TITLE: Investigating the Limitations of the Bernstein-von Mises Theorem in Large-Margin Regime
PROPOSAL: Analyze the convergence of the Bayesian posterior to the maximum likelihood estimate under the large-margin regime, where the loss function is bounded away from zero with a minimum margin. Specifically, we will derive a lower bound on the Bayesian posterior variance that captures the effect of the minimum margin.
CONTROLS: Compare to the classical Bernstein-von Mises theorem for finite-dimensional parameter spaces with an infinite-dimensional parameter space using a sparse prior.
COST: 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the posterior variance to converge to the inverse of the Fisher information matrix at a slower rate due to the minimum margin effect, illustrating the limitations of the Bernstein-von Mises theorem in this regime and motivating further investigation. This result may not hold for models with a small margin, where the Bayes uncertainty may still vanish.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: A New Path Integral Representation of Bayesian Neural Networks
PROPOSAL: Derive a path integral representation of Bayesian neural networks by approximating the posterior distribution as a sample average of neural network losses under random weight samples. This representation will enable efficient computation of the posterior predictive distribution without the need for expensive function evaluations.
CONTROLS: Compare to existing variational inference methods and exact Bayesian neural network computations for a range of architectures and datasets.
COST: 1000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect significant speedup and improved accuracy of the predictive distribution compared to existing variational inference methods, especially in large-scale settings. However, this method may not perform well if the weight distribution is highly concentrated around a single point, making the path integral representation less accurate.

TITLE: A New Path Integral Representation of Bayesian Neural Networks
PROPOSAL: Revising proposal 2 to focus on a more specific aspect: develop a path integral representation that minimizes the KL-divergence between the path integral and the true posterior, using a relaxation of the KL-divergence that can be optimized using stochastic gradient descent.
CONTROLS: Compare to existing path integral methods and MCMC approaches for approximating the Bayesian neural network posterior, including evaluation of the relaxed KL-divergence and the corresponding approximate posterior.
COST: 500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the new method to provide a more accurate approximation of the Bayesian neural network posterior, especially in cases where the true posterior is concentrated around a few modes. However, this method may be computationally expensive due to the need for stochastic gradient descent optimization.

PROPOSAL: Investigate the effect of prior shrinkage on the performance of Bayesian neural networks using synthetic datasets with varying amounts of overparameterization. We will examine how the choice of prior distribution affects the learned representations, predictive performance, and robustness to model misspecification.
CONTROLS: Compare to baseline models with uninformative priors and other regularization methods, including L1 and L2 regularization.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Regularized Posterior Embeddings for Valid Frequentist Coverage
PROPOSAL: Develop a method to construct regularized posterior embeddings that preserve the valid frequentist coverage of Bayesian predictive intervals in overparameterized settings. This will involve introducing a regularization term that penalizes the posterior variance, ensuring that the predictive intervals maintain their frequentist coverage properties.
CONTROLS: Compare to existing approaches for constructing Bayesian predictive intervals, including bootstrapped Bayesian predictive intervals and frequentist-CRAMER (Credible-member Random set Adjusted for Multiple Evaluations Relative) intervals.
COST: 400 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the regularized posterior embeddings to provide Bayesian predictive intervals with valid frequentist coverage, even in overparameterized settings where traditional Bayesian methods may fail. However, the regularization term may introduce bias, and its strength may need to be carefully tuned.

TITLE: Information-Theoretic Analysis of Bayesian Uncertainty in Deep Learning
PROPOSAL: Derive an information-theoretic lower bound on the Bayes risk of a Bayesian neural network, characterizing the optimal trade-off between predictive accuracy and uncertainty estimation in deep learning. This will involve developing a new framework that connects Bayesian neural networks to information-theoretic principles.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the derived lower bound using synthetic and real-world datasets, comparing it to existing state-of-the-art Bayesian neural network methods.
COST: 1200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the information-theoretic lower bound to provide new insights into the relationship between predictive accuracy and uncertainty estimation in Bayesian neural networks, motivating the development of new methods that achieve optimal trade-offs. However, deriving tighter bounds may require additional assumptions or modeling choices.

PROPOSAL: Develop a unified framework that combines the insights from the previous proposals to provide a comprehensive solution for achieving valid frequentist coverage in Bayesian neural networks. This will involve integrating the regularized posterior embeddings, information-theoretic analysis, and Bernstein-von Mises theorem extensions into a single framework.

However, implementing the framework may require additional development and tuning, and its performance may depend on the specific choice of hyperparameters.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Bernstein-Von Mises Theorem for Over-Parametrized Neural Networks
PROPOSAL: Investigate the validity of the Bernstein-Von Mises theorem in over-parametrized neural networks, specifically examining whether the posterior distribution asymptotically converges to a Gaussian centered at the maximum likelihood estimate, even in regimes where the data is scarce relative to the number of parameters.
CONTROLS: Baseline experiment comparing to the result of a standard implementation of the Bernstein-Von Mises theorem using finite-dimensional parameter spaces.
COST: 10 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The result will demonstrate that the Bernstein-Von Mises theorem does not hold in over-parametrized neural networks, with the posterior distribution deviating significantly from a Gaussian centered at the maximum likelihood estimate, thus highlighting the limitations of the theorem in modern machine learning scenarios. However, the result might not provide clear guidance on how to choose a suitable prior for a given problem.

However, the influence of the prior on the posterior might be mitigated by regularization techniques.

TITLE: Safe Bayesian Updating and Overcounting Evidence
PROPOSAL: Investigate the effect of overcounting evidence on Bayesian neural networks, specifically examining whether the information-processing optimality of Bayesian updating is violated when the evidence is overcounted. We will use a controlled setup where the true generating process is known and the data is synthetic.
CONTROLS: Experiment 1 (Bernstein-Von Mises Theorem for Over-Parametrized Neural Networks) as baseline; comparison with frequentist estimates.
COST: 30 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The result will demonstrate that overcounting evidence does indeed violate the information-processing optimality of Bayesian updating, confirming previous results, but with the added insight that the effect is more pronounced in over-parametrized models.

PROPOSAL: Develop a method to quantify the quality of priors using expected Kullback-Leibler distance, and apply it to Bayesian neural networks in an over-parametrized setting. This will provide an objective criterion for evaluating prior choices.
CONTROLS: Experiments 1, 2 (Inconsistent Posteriors with Influential Priors), and 3 (Safe Bayesian Updating and Overcounting Evidence) as baselines.
COST: 80 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The result will demonstrate that the expected Kullback-Leibler distance can be used as a useful metric for evaluating prior quality, with better priors leading to improved posterior distributions. However, the result might not provide clear guidance on how to choose a distribution for the Kullback-Leibler distance.

CONTROLS: Experiment 3 (Safe Bayesian Updating and Overcounting Evidence) as baseline; comparison with standard Bayesian methods and frequentist bootstrap methods.
